problems.title: Parking lot system
problems.ask: Design a parking lot system. Multiple floors, multiple spot types (compact/regular/large/electric-with-charger). Customers enter via a gate (ticket), park, and pay on exit. Make it extensible to add new spot types and pricing strategies.

sources.ref: LDDD Ch.2-3 — aggregates and bounded contexts

deep_dive_targets: Spot allocation strategy (nearest-first vs first-available vs vehicle-type-aware)
Pricing strategy (flat rate vs tiered vs dynamic)
follow_ups: Add electric vehicle charging — how does this land?
Add monthly subscribers who skip payment — what changes?
Multi-lot operator: 50 lots across a city. Where's the seam?
problems.trap_for_juniors: Conflating spot selection with pricing — collapsing them into one class. They change for different reasons (spot choice = layout, pricing = business model). Two separate Strategy interfaces.

problems.title: Elevator bank scheduler
problems.ask: Design the system that controls a bank of 4 elevators in a 20-floor building. Riders press call buttons; elevators pick up and drop off. Write the classes, the scheduling algorithm, and make it thread-safe.

uses_for: ElevatorBank as aggregate root with Elevators as entities

deep_dive_targets: Scheduling algorithm (FCFS vs LOOK vs SCAN vs nearest-car)
Concurrency model (channels per elevator vs central mutex)
follow_ups: Add emergency stop — preempts all current motion.
VIP rider — guarantees under 30s wait time.
How do you test this deterministically (no real wall-clock)?
problems.trap_for_juniors: Treating each elevator independently and having the request hit a random one. The win is the *bank* sees the request, scheduler decides which car takes it. Per-elevator scheduling = N elevators × O(N) bad decisions.

problems.title: Vending machine
problems.ask: Design a vending machine. Coins/notes in, item dispensed, change out. Handle out-of-stock, insufficient funds, cancel mid-transaction. Pure state machine.
deep_dive_targets: State machine: idle → coin-accepted → item-selected → dispensing → idle (with cancel paths)
Change-making algorithm (greedy fails for non-canonical denominations; DP is correct)
follow_ups: Add card payments — how does the state machine extend?
Coin jam mid-dispense — how do you recover?
Multiple vending machines, central inventory — what changes?
problems.trap_for_juniors: Using nested if/else for the state machine. As states grow it becomes unreadable. State pattern: each state is a class that handles its own transitions; adding a state doesn't touch existing code.

problems.title: Tic-Tac-Toe (extensible to N×N)
problems.ask: Design Tic-Tac-Toe. Two players, 3×3 grid. Now extend to N×N where you need K-in-a-row to win. Keep the win-check efficient as N grows.
deep_dive_targets: Win-check optimization: O(N²) naive vs O(N) incremental (track row/col/diag counts)
Open-Closed extension to Connect-4 / Gomoku without rewriting the engine
follow_ups: Make it Connect-4 (gravity!) — what changes in the design?
Add Gomoku (15×15, 5-in-a-row) — where does it land?
How would you add an AI opponent (minimax) without coupling to the game class?
problems.trap_for_juniors: Hardcoding win patterns. For 3×3 there are 8; for N×N there are 4N+2. Naive enumeration is O(N²); incremental tracking (counters per row/col/diag updated on each move) is O(1) per move.

problems.title: Splitwise (expense splitter)
problems.ask: Design Splitwise. Users add expenses with arbitrary split (equal, percentage, exact). The system shows simplified balances ('A owes B $X') across many transactions. Support 'settle up' to reset two users' debt.

uses_for: Expense as event, Balance as projection

deep_dive_targets: Debt simplification algorithm (transitive closure → minimum cash flow)
Domain model: Expense vs Balance vs Settlement (which is the source of truth?)
follow_ups: Multiple currencies — when do you convert?
Group expenses with 50 members — simplification gets quadratic; how do you bound it?
Concurrent expense additions by two users — how do you avoid double-counting on settlement?
problems.trap_for_juniors: Storing balances directly and mutating them. Expenses are the source of truth — balance is a projection. If you mutate balances, you can never reconstruct, audit, or simplify.

problems.title: Token-aware rate limiter for an agent fleet
problems.ask: Design a thread-safe rate limiter for an inference API consumed by a tool-calling agent that fans out into thousands of concurrent sub-agents. Limit on BOTH tokens-per-minute (TPM) and requests-per-minute (RPM), keyed by (caller_identity × endpoint × tier). It must be FAIR — one runaway sub-agent cannot starve the rest of the fleet. On reject, return a 429 with a correct Retry-After. Start single-process, then make it distributed.

sources.ref: Cloudflare — How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains
Stripe — Scaling your API with rate limiters

uses_for: why wall-clock windows drift across nodes

deep_dive_targets: Limiting on TOKENS not requests: reserve-then-reconcile (you don't know output token count until generation completes) vs pre-charge worst case
Fairness across N sub-agents: weighted fair queuing / deficit round robin vs naive shared token bucket (and the global-mutex contention it creates)
follow_ups: Cost-of-service framing: this limit is a function of (caller × endpoint × tier × per-token GPU cost) — derive the number before the algorithm.
Distributed version: Redis token bucket with Lua atomicity — what breaks when Redis is the bottleneck?
A burst of 5000 sub-agents wakes simultaneously — thundering herd on the shared counter. How do you shard it?
problems.trap_for_juniors: Counting requests instead of tokens — a single 200k-token prompt costs more than 1000 tiny calls, so RPM limiting alone lets one caller melt the fleet. And: one global mutex around the counter serializes every sub-agent, defeating the concurrency you were hired to protect.

problems.title: SnapshotSet (versioned set with snapshot iterators)
problems.ask: Design a SnapshotSet: a mutable set of unique keys supporting add(k), remove(k), contains(k), and iterator(). iterator() returns a SNAPSHOT — adds/removes performed after the iterator is created must NOT be visible to it, and multiple snapshots taken at different points can be iterated independently and concurrently. Minimize the space overhead of keeping many snapshots alive. Then make the whole thing thread-safe for concurrent readers and writers.

uses_for: each snapshot sees a consistent version
structural sharing as the alternative to per-element version tags

deep_dive_targets: Versioned visibility: tag each element with (addedVer, removedVer) and represent a snapshot as a single integer version V; the iterator yields k iff addedVer(k) ≤ V < removedVer(k) — derive why this makes iterator() O(1) and gives snapshot isolation with zero copying

Space reclamation across many live snapshots: track the oldest live snapshot version and GC tombstones no snapshot can still see (the MVCC VACUUM problem), plus the thread-safe read path (RWMutex vs an atomic version-pointer + COW) so readers never block the writer
follow_ups: 1000 live snapshots each differing by one element — a full copy is O(N) per snapshot. How do version tags or structural sharing bound the cost?
A snapshot iterator is held open for an hour while writes pour in — what stops the dead-version list from growing without bound? (the long-running-reader / VACUUM-can't-advance bug)
Make iteration itself lock-free by snapshotting the version and walking an immutable structure — what consistency do you actually guarantee mid-iteration?
problems.trap_for_juniors: Deep-copying the whole set inside iterator() — O(N) time and memory per snapshot, so 100 snapshots of a 1M-element set materializes 100M elements. Snapshot isolation comes from versioning (an integer + per-element version tags) or structural sharing, never copying. And freeing a tombstoned element while an older snapshot can still see it corrupts that snapshot — exactly the MVCC vacuum-too-early bug.

problems.title: DDSketch — mergeable streaming quantile sketch
problems.ask: Implement a streaming quantile sketch: add(value) and quantile(q) over a stream of millions of latency measurements, in BOUNDED memory, with a configurable RELATIVE error guarantee (the returned p99 is within, say, 1% of the true p99 across a 1ms-to-60s range). It must be MERGEABLE: per-host sketches combine into one sketch answering quantiles over the union, so percentiles are computed in a distributed fashion. Keep memory bounded even on heavy-tailed inputs.

sources.ref: Masson, Rim, Lee 2019 (VLDB) — DDSketch: A Fast and Fully-Mergeable Quantile Sketch with Relative-Error Guarantees
Datadog — Computing accurate percentiles with DDSketch
uses_for: 10× faster than GK, as fast as HDR

deep_dive_targets: The logarithmic bucket mapping: index i = ⌈log_γ(x)⌉ with γ = (1+α)/(1−α); bucket i covers [γ^i, γ^{i+1}) so any value in it is within relative error α of its representative — derive why log-spaced buckets give RELATIVE (not absolute) error, and walk inserting 1, 100, 10000 to show the index growing by ~constant steps

Mergeability + bounded memory: two sketches with the SAME γ have aligned indices, so merge = elementwise sum of bucket counts in O(#buckets); derive why a fixed γ is the precondition for distributed pre-aggregation, and how collapsing the lowest-count buckets caps memory on heavy tails without breaking the tail-quantile guarantee
follow_ups: Compare to t-digest and GK (Greenwald-Khanna): why does DDSketch give relative-error guarantees they don't, and where does t-digest still win?
quantile(0.5) needs the bucket where the cumulative count crosses N/2 — derive the O(#buckets) scan, and why #buckets = O(log(max/min)/log γ), not O(N)
The log map is undefined at 0 and for x<0 — how do you handle negatives and exact zeros (a mirrored negative store + a dedicated zero counter)?
problems.trap_for_juniors: Storing every value (or a wide fixed-width linear histogram) to compute percentiles — O(N) memory, and a linear histogram gives ABSOLUTE error, useless across a heavy-tailed 1ms-to-60s range. And merging two sketches built with different γ: the buckets don't align so the merge is silently wrong. Mergeability REQUIRES a shared mapping.

problems.title: Time-windowed log/event store with range query
problems.ask: Design an in-memory store for timestamped log events. ingest(ts, event) appends; query(start, end) returns events in that time range in order; data older than a retention horizon is dropped. Ingest is high-throughput and mostly-but-not-strictly increasing in time (late/out-of-order events happen). Make range queries sub-linear, retention O(1), and the whole thing safe under concurrent ingest + query.

uses_for: retention = drop oldest segment, not delete-from-front

sources.ref: Prometheus TSDB — head block + WAL + sealed blocks
uses_for: mutable head vs immutable sealed blocks

deep_dive_targets: Time-bucketed index: partition the timeline into fixed-duration buckets (e.g. 1-min shards); query(start,end) touches only ⌈(end−start)/bucket⌉ buckets and binary-searches the two edges — derive O(log n + k) vs O(N) flat scan, and why retention becomes an O(1) unlink-oldest-bucket instead of an O(N) delete

Concurrent ingest + query with out-of-order events: one mutable 'hot' bucket taking appends vs immutable 'sealed' buckets readers scan lock-free, and a watermark deciding when a bucket may seal despite late arrivals — walk an event landing 90s late and where it goes
follow_ups: An event arrives 10 minutes late but its bucket was already sealed and evicted — accept into a side-bucket, reject, or reopen? What does the business actually want?
A 24h query over 1-min buckets touches 1440 buckets — when do you roll up into coarser buckets (downsampling), and what accuracy do you trade?
Make sealed-segment reads truly lock-free: how does an immutable segment + atomic pointer swap on seal get you there?
problems.trap_for_juniors: One flat slice sorted by time behind a mutex — every query is O(N) and retention is an O(N) delete-from-front that fights ingest for the lock. Time-bucketing turns range queries into a handful of bucket scans and retention into an O(1) unlink. And assuming timestamps are strictly increasing — late events then break the sort invariant or get silently dropped.

problems.title: Time-based versioned key-value store (TimeMap)
problems.ask: Design a TimeMap: set(key, value, ts) stores a versioned value, and get(key, ts) returns the value with the largest stored timestamp ≤ ts (empty if none). It must answer point-in-time reads efficiently as each key accumulates thousands of versions, support TTL/compaction of old versions, and be thread-safe for concurrent set/get.

uses_for: reading the version visible at a timestamp
this is the MVCC read path

deep_dive_targets: Per-key array sorted by timestamp + binary search for the largest ts ≤ query (upper_bound then step back one) — derive O(log v) get and O(1) amortized append WHEN writes are timestamp-monotonic, vs O(v) insertion when a write arrives out of order; name the adversarial out-of-order write that degrades it

Thread-safe + bounded memory: append-only per-key slices sharded by key hash under RWMutex (concurrent readers, appending writer), plus TTL/compaction that drops versions past the horizon — and why this IS the MVCC read path (Postgres/HBase store the same timestamp-versioned cells)
follow_ups: get is 100× more frequent than set — does a copy-on-write append (immutable per-key snapshot) beat locking? What does it cost the writer?
A key has 1M versions but reads only ever ask for the last hour — how does tiered storage / compaction keep the hot array small?
Two sets race with the same (key, ts) — last-writer-wins, reject, or store both? What does the timestamp even mean then?
problems.trap_for_juniors: Storing map[key][]value and linear-scanning for the right timestamp — O(v) per get, so a hot key with 10k versions makes every read 10k comparisons. Keep versions sorted and binary-search. And assuming set() always arrives in timestamp order — one out-of-order write breaks the sorted invariant the binary search depends on, returning wrong values silently.

problems.title: Streaming heavy-hitters / top-K (Count-Min Sketch)
problems.ask: Design a streaming top-K: over a high-rate stream of keys (request paths, customer IDs) with billions of distinct values, answer 'what are the K most frequent keys right now?' in BOUNDED memory — you cannot keep a counter per distinct key. Tolerate a small over-count error. Then extend to a sliding window (top-K over the last 5 minutes) and make it mergeable across shards.

sources.ref: Cormode & Muthukrishnan 2005 — An Improved Data Stream Summary: the Count-Min Sketch
Datadog — top-N endpoints by traffic over a window
uses_for: why exact per-key counters don't fit

deep_dive_targets: The d×w counter matrix: d independent hash functions, each key increments one counter per row, estimate = MIN across the d rows — derive why MIN cancels collisions (collisions only ADD, so the min row is least-polluted) and the bound w = ⌈e/ε⌉, d = ⌈ln 1/δ⌉; walk two colliding keys through it

Top-K on top of CMS: a size-K min-heap of (key, estimate); on each update estimate the key and conditionally sift it in — derive why CMS alone can't enumerate heavy hitters (it stores no key list) so you need the heap beside it, and a ring of per-bucket sketches you sum + expire for the sliding window
follow_ups: Compare to SpaceSaving / Misra-Gries (deterministic, bounded counters) — when does the exact-ish counter approach beat CMS + heap?
Merge across 100 shards: CMS matrices with the same hashes and dimensions sum elementwise — derive why mergeability needs identical hash seeds (mirroring DDSketch's fixed-γ requirement)
CMS only ever over-counts, never under — what does that mean for a heavy hitter you're about to alert on? Can a cold key ever look hot?
problems.trap_for_juniors: A hashmap of key→count — exact but O(distinct keys) memory, unbounded when keys are URLs or user IDs. CMS trades a small over-count for fixed memory. And using a single hash row: collisions then inflate estimates with no way to cancel — the d-row MIN is the whole point. Also CMS has no key list, so 'top-K' needs a heap alongside it.

problems.title: BPE tokenizer (encode/decode with byte fallback)
problems.ask: Implement a tokenizer: encode(text) -> []int and decode([]int) -> text, driven by a vocab + ordered merge rules (byte-pair encoding). Critically: characters/bytes NOT covered by the vocab keys (emoji, rare scripts) must still round-trip losslessly via byte fallback, so tokenize ∘ detokenize is the identity. Keep encode efficient as the text grows.

sources.ref: Sennrich et al. 2016 — Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units

deep_dive_targets: The merge loop as a data-structure problem: symbols in a doubly-linked list + a heap of adjacent pairs keyed by merge RANK — derive why it's O(n log n), not greedy longest-match
Byte fallback: representing the 256 raw bytes as base tokens so any UTF-8 input is always encodable, and why naive char-level vocab crashes on unseen codepoints
follow_ups: Streaming decode: a token boundary splits a multi-byte UTF-8 character — how do you emit only complete runes?
Add special tokens (<|im_start|>) that must never be split by BPE — where do they intercept the pipeline?
Two different token sequences decode to the same string — is that a bug?
problems.trap_for_juniors: Greedy longest-match against the vocab instead of replaying merges in rank order — produces a different (wrong) tokenization than the model was trained on. And assuming every input char is in the vocab → KeyError/panic on the first emoji.

problems.title: Continuous-batching scheduler (LLM inference)
problems.ask: Design the scheduler that feeds one GPU model executor. Requests arrive continuously with prompts of varying length. Implement iteration-level (continuous) batching: admit new requests into the running batch and retire finished sequences EVERY decode step — don't wait for a static batch to fill. Respect a fixed KV-cache memory budget. Maximize throughput without starving short requests.

sources.ref: Yu et al. 2022 (OSDI) — Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models
Kwon et al. 2023 (SOSP) — Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention (vLLM)
vLLM docs — continuous batching & chunked prefill

deep_dive_targets: The decode loop as a state machine: running set + waiting queue, per-step admit/evict gated on free KV blocks — walk three requests of length 5, 200, 12 through it
Prefill vs decode cost asymmetry and chunked prefill: derive the max batch size from (KV bytes per token × budget), and why head-of-line blocking appears without iteration-level scheduling
follow_ups: Prefix caching: 1000 requests share a 2k-token system prompt — how does the scheduler exploit that?
SLO classes: an interactive request must not wait behind a 100k-token batch job. Priority + preemption?
Out of KV mid-decode: preempt-and-recompute vs swap-to-CPU — which, when?
problems.trap_for_juniors: Static batching — waiting for N requests before launching. A 4k-token straggler then blocks 31 finished slots, and the GPU idles. Iteration-level scheduling admits/retires per step. Also: ignoring the KV budget → OOM mid-generation, the worst possible time to fail.

problems.title: Agent orchestration loop + tool dispatcher
problems.ask: Design the core runtime of an LLM agent. The control loop is observe → think (model call) → act (tool call) → observe, repeating until a termination condition. A tool registry maps tool name → typed schema + handler; dispatch must validate the model's arguments against the schema, execute with a timeout + sandbox, parse the result, and feed structured errors back to the model. Bound the loop (max steps, token/cost budget). Make tools pluggable and some tool calls run in parallel.

sources.ref: Yao et al. 2023 — ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models

deep_dive_targets: The loop as a state machine with explicit termination set (final answer / max steps / budget exhausted / hard error) — why an unbounded loop is the #1 production incident
Tool dispatch internals: registry → JSON-schema arg validation → timeout + sandbox → structured error back to the model, plus bounded-concurrency parallel tool calls
follow_ups: A tool is non-idempotent (send_email) and the step is retried after a timeout — how do you avoid double-send?
Stream partial tool output back into the loop before the tool finishes — what changes?
Human-in-the-loop: pause before a destructive tool, persist state, resume later. Where's the seam?
problems.trap_for_juniors: No max-steps and no budget ceiling — the agent loops forever or burns thousands of dollars on one request. And executing the model's tool arguments without schema validation — the model hallucinates a field and your handler panics or, worse, does the wrong destructive thing.

problems.title: SSE token-streaming multiplexer
problems.ask: Design the server component that streams generated tokens to clients token-by-token over Server-Sent Events. One generation may fan out to multiple subscribers (tabs, observers). Clients can disconnect or cancel — and if the LAST subscriber leaves, generation should stop (it's burning GPU). A slow client must never block the generator or the other clients. Support resume-from-offset on reconnect.

sources.ref: OpenAI API streaming docs — SSE token stream format

uses_for: producer/consumer signalling for the per-subscriber buffer

deep_dive_targets: Slow-consumer problem: per-subscriber bounded ring buffer + drop-or-disconnect policy, so the generator (single producer) never blocks on the slowest client
Cancellation propagation: refcount subscribers; last unsubscribe cancels the generation context — walk the bytes/IDs of a resume-from-offset reconnect
follow_ups: TTFT vs throughput: do you flush every token or coalesce? What does buffering cost the user?
SSE vs WebSocket here — what does each buy, and which for one-directional token push?
Exactly-once token delivery across a reconnect — sequence IDs and dedup. Is exactly-once even achievable?
problems.trap_for_juniors: A single writer that does a blocking write to each client in turn — one slow client stalls everyone, and TTFT for fast clients collapses. Fan out through bounded per-subscriber channels. And: no cancellation, so the GPU keeps generating after every client has left.

problems.title: KV-cache block manager (PagedAttention-style)
problems.ask: Implement the allocator that manages GPU KV-cache as fixed-size blocks, like OS pages. Each sequence requests blocks as it grows during decoding. Support prefix sharing: many sequences with a common prompt point at the same physical blocks (copy-on-write when they diverge). Support eviction/preemption under memory pressure. alloc and free are O(1).

uses_for: the OS analogy the whole design borrows

deep_dive_targets: Free-list block allocator (O(1) alloc/free) + per-sequence block table (logical block → physical block) — walk a sequence growing from 1 to 3 blocks
Refcounted shared blocks with copy-on-write: two sequences share a prompt prefix, then one writes — derive when you copy vs share, and the bug when you free a still-referenced block
follow_ups: Memory pressure: swap blocks to CPU RAM vs drop-and-recompute on resume — cost model for each.
Beam search forks a sequence into k beams — how does CoW make that cheap?
Internal fragmentation: last block of every sequence is partially full — how big should a block be?
problems.trap_for_juniors: Allocating one contiguous KV region per sequence sized to max length — the pre-vLLM mistake. You waste 60-80% to internal fragmentation and OOM far below real capacity. Paging into fixed blocks is the fix. And: freeing a block whose refcount > 1 corrupts another sequence's cache.

problems.title: Meeting scheduler / calendar
problems.ask: Design a calendar scheduling system. Users propose meetings with N participants; the system finds the next slot where everyone is free. Each user has working hours, time zones, and existing events.
deep_dive_targets: Interval tree for fast 'find next free slot of duration D' query
Multi-participant scheduling: intersection of N free-busy lists in O(N log M)
follow_ups: Add recurring events — how do you store them efficiently?
Add 'optional attendees' — does the algorithm change?
How do you handle daylight saving transitions?
problems.trap_for_juniors: Storing events as a flat list and scanning linearly. At 10k events per user, every scheduling query is O(N²). Interval tree (or red-black-tree with augmented data) brings it to O(log N).

problems.title: Logging framework
problems.ask: Design a logging framework like log4j or zap. Multiple log levels, multiple output destinations (file, network, stdout), structured logging with key-value pairs, and pluggable formatters. Thread-safe.

sources.ref: Head First Design Patterns — CoR chapter

deep_dive_targets: Appender chain (filter → format → write) and lifecycle
Zero-allocation structured logging (sync.Pool, encoder reuse)
follow_ups: Add async logging — write to a buffer, flush in background. What can break?
Add log sampling — keep 1% of debug logs but 100% of errors.
How do you handle a slow downstream (network appender blocks)?
problems.trap_for_juniors: Synchronous writes inside the application thread. At high log rates, the slow appender (network, file) blocks the hot path. Async logging with a bounded buffer + drop policy is the production answer.

problems.title: LRU cache (thread-safe)
problems.ask: Design an LRU cache with O(1) get and put. Capacity N. Now make it thread-safe — multiple goroutines/threads accessing concurrently. Discuss the lock contention trade-off and how you'd reduce it.

sources.ref: Cloudflare — sharded LRU cache for high concurrency

deep_dive_targets: Doubly-linked list + hashmap composition (the O(1) trick)
Lock striping: from one mutex to N shards, contention reduction analysis
follow_ups: Add TTL — what changes?
Replace LRU with LFU — what stays, what breaks?
Make it persistent across restarts (with eventual consistency to disk).
problems.trap_for_juniors: Putting a single mutex around the whole cache. At high concurrency, every reader serializes — defeats the cache. Lock striping (shard the cache, mutex per shard) cuts contention by N. Lock-free designs exist but are interview-tier-only.

problems.title: Thread pool / executor
problems.ask: Design a thread pool. N workers, a queue of submitted tasks, graceful shutdown, and the ability to submit a Future-style result. Show how you'd implement work-stealing for load balancing.
deep_dive_targets: Work-stealing: per-worker deque, victim selection, LIFO own / FIFO steal
Graceful shutdown: drain queue, signal workers, await Done — without losing in-flight tasks
follow_ups: Add priority — a high-priority task should jump the queue.
Add bounded queue — what's the back-pressure strategy?
Add cancellation — how do tasks observe cancel without polling?
problems.trap_for_juniors: Single shared task queue with a mutex. Becomes a contention point at high task rates. Work-stealing (per-worker deque) reduces contention dramatically — workers push/pop their own deque LIFO; only steal from others when empty.

problems.title: In-memory file system
problems.ask: Design an in-memory file system. Directories, files, file contents. Support ls, mkdir, addContentToFile, readContentFromFile. Tree structure with arbitrary nesting.

sources.ref: Head First Design Patterns — Composite chapter

deep_dive_targets: Composite pattern: File and Directory share a common interface; tree operations are recursive
Path resolution algorithm and edge cases (`/`, `.`, `..`, trailing slashes)
follow_ups: Add symbolic links — how do you avoid cycles?
Add permissions (read/write/execute) — where do they live?
Make it persistent (snapshot to disk) — what serialization shape?
problems.trap_for_juniors: Using two separate hierarchies for files and directories. Composite pattern unifies them under one Node interface — `ls` doesn't care whether a child is a file or a sub-directory; it just calls `name()`.

problems.title: In-memory pub-sub
problems.ask: Design an in-memory publish-subscribe system. Publishers send messages to a topic; subscribers receive messages for topics they've subscribed to. Support wildcard subscriptions (`logs.*` matches `logs.error` and `logs.info`). Thread-safe.
deep_dive_targets: Topic tree for wildcard matching (trie of topic segments)
Slow subscriber problem: per-subscriber bounded channel + drop policy
follow_ups: Add durability — survive a process restart.
Add ordered delivery per topic — what synchronization is needed?
Scale to 10k subscribers per topic — what changes?
problems.trap_for_juniors: Letting a slow subscriber block the publisher. One subscriber that doesn't drain its queue halts message delivery to everyone. Bounded per-subscriber channels with drop-or-disconnect policy is the answer.

problems.title: Undo/Redo (text editor)
problems.ask: Design the undo/redo system for a text editor. Operations include insert, delete, format. Memory-bounded history (last N operations). Now extend to collaborative editing where one user's undo doesn't undo another user's work.
deep_dive_targets: Command pattern: each operation knows how to apply + reverse itself
Selective undo in collaborative editing (the OT/CRDT problem)
follow_ups: How do you handle 'undo' after the document was edited remotely?
Memory: insert of a 1MB image — do you store it in history?
What about non-undoable side effects (send email, file upload)?
problems.trap_for_juniors: Storing whole-document snapshots for each undo step. At 1KB doc × 10k operations, that's 10MB. Command pattern stores only the *delta* + reverse-delta — O(operation-size) per step.

problems.title: Thread-safe blocking queue
problems.ask: Implement a thread-safe blocking queue with bounded capacity. `put` blocks when full; `take` blocks when empty. Multiple producers and consumers. Now make it fair (FIFO across threads, not just elements).
deep_dive_targets: Two condition variables (notFull, notEmpty) and the wait/signal protocol
Fairness: ReentrantLock(fair=true) vs unfair — semantic and perf trade-off
follow_ups: Implement it in Go using only channels — what changes?
Add timeout to put/take — what's the API and the cancellation semantics?
What if `take` is called with a predicate (only take messages matching X)?
problems.trap_for_juniors: Using `Object.notify()` instead of `notifyAll()` (Java) or signal-one instead of broadcast. Causes deadlock when multiple consumers wait on the same condition. Always use `notifyAll`/`Broadcast` unless you can prove only one waiter needs waking.

problems.title: Circuit breaker
problems.ask: Design a circuit breaker (Netflix Hystrix style). Calls to a downstream service can fail; once failures exceed a threshold, the breaker opens and short-circuits subsequent calls. After a cooldown, it tries again (half-open state).
deep_dive_targets: Three-state machine: Closed → Open → HalfOpen → Closed (with thresholds)
Rolling window for failure counting (vs cumulative — accuracy/memory trade-off)
follow_ups: What metric drives the transition? (Failure count, failure rate, latency, all of the above?)
How do you handle the 'thundering herd' when the breaker closes?
Multiple downstream services — one breaker each or one shared?
problems.trap_for_juniors: Using a cumulative failure counter. At sustained low failure rate, you eventually trip even though the service is healthy. Sliding window (last N seconds) is the production answer.

problems.title: Workflow engine (DAG of tasks)
problems.ask: Design a workflow engine. Users define a DAG of tasks (Task A → Task B, C; Task D depends on B and C). Workers execute tasks; the engine tracks state, handles retries, and signals completion. Tasks may produce outputs consumed by downstream tasks.
deep_dive_targets: Topological execution with concurrent ready-task pool
Retry semantics: at-least-once vs exactly-once via idempotency keys + deterministic replay
follow_ups: A task succeeds but the engine crashes before recording success — what happens?
How do you handle a task that runs for 7 days (vs 7 ms)?
Dynamic DAGs (a task discovers new tasks at runtime) — what changes?
problems.trap_for_juniors: Treating tasks as ad-hoc function calls. Workflow engines must be *deterministic* — given the same inputs, replay produces the same result. This requires capturing all non-determinism (time, random, external calls) in the workflow state, not the task logic.
